title: The patient farmer (James 5:7–12)
hookLine: the farmer waits for the early and late rain

lines: YOU CAN'T YELL A SEED UP.
THE EARLY RAIN, THE LATTER RAIN.
cards: You can't make a seed grow faster by yelling at it. You plant, you water, and then you wait, and the waiting is most of the work. The Bible speaks of two rains in that land, the early rain and the latter rain.
Commentators place the early one in autumn, softening hard ground for plowing and sowing, and the latter in spring, swelling the grain before harvest. Between them, months of watching the sky.
James has just thundered at the rich who cheated their workers. Now he turns to his brethren, people waiting for things to be put right, and gives them a farmer to look at.

teach.b: In the King James Bible: "Be patient therefore, brethren, unto the coming of the Lord. Behold, the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it, until he receive the early and latter rain."
Husbandman is the old word for farmer. And his patience isn't idle. Farmers weed, mend fences and fix the plow, but they can't make it rain.
Be patient like that, James says, and steady your hearts, because the coming of the Lord is near.
Then a warning for people under strain: "Grudge not one against another." Long waiting turns people on each other. Look, the judge is standing at the door.
Then two more pictures of endurance. The prophets, who spoke for God and suffered for it. And: "Ye have heard of the patience of Job."
Patient as Job, people say. Yet in the book of Job, he doesn't sit quietly. He argues, laments and demands an answer from God.

teach.h: JOB: LOUD, BUT HE DIDN'T LET GO.
teach.b: The Greek word James uses here means endurance, staying under the weight, and that is exactly what Job did: he complained loudly, and he didn't let go.
You've seen how it ended, James says: the Lord is full of pity and mercy. Last, a word about honesty: don't swear oaths.
"Let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay."
While you wait on God, keep your word plain. That closes a week in James, from faith and works and the tongue to the patient farmer.

how: James 5:7–10 is an Advent reading in some church lectionaries, in the season of waiting before Christmas, and Christians often turn to it in long illnesses or hard seasons.

o: a prophet who called down rain after a long drought
a man who suffered in silence and never once complained
a man whose patience meant arguing with God but holding on

games.q: what's inside James 5:7–12 — tap the pairs.

s: the patience of Job means he never complained
he argued and lamented loudly. the Greek word means endurance: he didn't let go.
the phrase 'the patience of Job' is in James
"Ye have heard of the patience of Job."
James warns that people who wait long turn on each other

games.q: you're a farmer. the seed is in, and the spring rain hasn't come yet. what do you do?
o: dig up the seed to check on it.
keep working what you can, and wait for the rain.
give up on this year's harvest.
games.why: "the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it, until he receive the early and latter rain."

practice: Think of something you're waiting on right now, a test result, a reply, a door that hasn't opened, and sort it into two piles like a farmer: the part you can work on, and the part that is rain, out of your hands.
Set the rain part down, breathe into the waiting without hurrying it, and notice any grudge rising toward someone in it. If you pray, ask for patience.

wordCard.voice: Job. The example James gives of patience that still argues and laments loudly, enduring under the weight without letting go of God.

orig.note: Greek: endurance, literally remaining under. the word James uses for the patience of Job.

carryVoice: Your line: be patient. The farmer works on what he can, and waits for the rain. See you tomorrow.
